newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Bosnian Serbs sign pact with Yugoslavia.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs sign pact with Yugoslavia.

text.p: Yugoslavia and the Bosnian Serb republic (RS) on Friday signed a comprehensive cooperation pact including a defence agreement, Tanjug news agency said.

The announcement said the arrangement would need to be ratified by the Bosnian parliament, which includes the Moslem-Croat federation, and did not violate the Dayton peace agreement which ended the Bosnian war.

The cooperation agreement was signed in Belgrade by Yugoslav President Zoran Lilic and Momcilo Krajisnik, the Bosnian Serb member of the Bosnian presidency in which all three ethnic communities are represented.
The RS Serb republic occupies half of Bosnian territory under the Dayton agreement and shares a border with the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.

Its leaders have made no secret of their desire to strengthen links with Yugoslavia despite the Dayton agreement which combines the Bosnian Serb republic with the Moslem-Croat federation in a sovereign Bosnia.
Bosnian Serbs began the war in 1992 in rebellion against Moslem and Croat-led Bosnian independence from former Yugoslavia.
The new cooperation agreement said Yugoslavia and the RS would develop common economic, foreign and legal policies and their citizens would have cross-border freedom of movement.
The clause on defence said neither side would allow its territory to be used for aggression against the other.
It set up a Cooperation Council to be headed by Lilic with Krajisnik as his deputy, although the RS has its own elected president in Mrs Biljana Plavsic.

Plavsic, who supported the Serbian opposition during its three month struggle to force President Slobodan Milosevic to accept his defeat in municipal elections last November, did not attend the signing ceremony.
Political sources said the rapprochement between Yugoslavia and the RS was part of Milosevic's efforts to repair the damage he and his Socialist party (SPS) suffered during the election dispute.
Milosevic angered the RS leadership when he forced them to accept the 1995 Dayton agreement against their will and is now struggling for his own political survival.
